opus-5.5.text:
Sure. So in Genie, the first step is that we don't operate directly on raw pixels for the dynamics model. We have a video tokenizer, which is a VQ-VAE style model built on a spatiotemporal transformer, that takes video frames and compresses each one into a grid of discrete tokens. Each token roughly corresponds to a patch of the image, so instead of predicting millions of pixel values, the dynamics model is predicting a much smaller set of discrete codes from a learned vocabulary.

The dynamics model itself is also a spatiotemporal transformer, and it's trained in a MaskGIT-like way. During training we take the tokens for a sequence of frames, randomly mask out some fraction of the tokens in the future frames, and ask the model to predict the masked ones. It conditions on the tokens from the past frames and on the latent action that was inferred between frames. That's the key piece. The latent action model, trained without any action labels, gives us a small discrete code that says, roughly, "here's what changed," and the dynamics model learns to use that code to decide what the next frame's tokens should be.

At inference time you start from an image, which you tokenize, and then a user or an agent picks one of the latent actions. The dynamics model then fills in the next frame's tokens iteratively. It predicts all the masked tokens, keeps the most confident ones, re-masks the rest, and repeats for a few steps. Then you decode those tokens back into pixels with the tokenizer's decoder, and you've got your next frame. You keep rolling that forward autoregressively, frame by frame.

One design choice that made a real difference was how we feed in the action. Instead of concatenating it as an extra token, we use it as an additive embedding, and that made the model much more controllable. The model actually pays attention to the action instead of just continuing whatever motion it sees in the history. And because the transformer factorizes attention over space and time, attending within a frame and then across frames at the same location, it stays tractable as you add more frames.

r001.rationale: The response says video patches are represented as discrete tokens and predicted, but it does not state that patch prediction uses cross-entropy loss.

r002.rationale: The response explicitly says the dynamics model is trained in a MaskGIT-like way by masking future-frame tokens and asking the model to predict them.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way to think about Genie is that it's really three pieces, and the dynamics model is the piece that sits in the middle and does the actual prediction. The first piece is a video tokenizer. We take raw video frames and run them through a VQ-VAE style encoder, so each frame gets chopped into patches and every patch gets mapped to a discrete code from a learned codebook. So instead of pixels, a frame becomes a grid of integer tokens. And importantly, that tokenizer is spatiotemporal, so it's looking at a little window of frames at once when it decides on those codes, which helps the tokens carry some motion information rather than just appearance.

The second piece is the latent action model, which is the part people tend to find most interesting. Because we're training on unlabeled internet video, we don't have action labels. So we learn a small discrete set of latent actions, something like eight codes, by looking at a frame and the next frame and asking, what's the minimal bit of information you'd need to explain the transition? That gets quantized through a very small codebook, and that bottleneck is what forces the actions to be meaningful and controllable.

Then the dynamics model is where the prediction happens. It's a transformer, specifically we use a spatiotemporal transformer in the style of ST-ViViT, where attention alternates between spatial layers that attend across the patches within a frame and temporal layers that attend across time for a given patch position. That factorization is what keeps the compute manageable, because if you did full attention over every token in every frame it blows up really quickly.

The input to the dynamics model is the sequence of frame tokens from the tokenizer, plus the latent action tokens, and we just add the action embedding to the frame tokens at each timestep. The training objective is a MaskGIT style one. So at each training step we randomly mask out some fraction of the tokens in the future frames, and the model has to predict the codebook index for each masked patch, conditioned on the past frames and the actions. It's a cross entropy loss over the codebook, token by token.

At inference time, that means generation is iterative rather than strictly autoregressive over patches. You start with a fully masked next frame, the model predicts a distribution for every patch, you keep the ones it's most confident about, re-mask the rest, and do that for a handful of steps. Then you decode those tokens back to pixels with the tokenizer's decoder. And because the action is just a token you feed in, a user can pick an action at every step and steer the video, which is really the whole point of the system.

r001.rationale: The response says each video patch is mapped to a discrete codebook token and that the dynamics model predicts masked patch codebook indices using a token-by-token cross-entropy loss.

r002.rationale: It explicitly describes randomly masking tokens in future frames during training and having the model predict the masked tokens.

astra-6.text:
The idea is to turn video prediction into a token prediction problem. We first use a video tokenizer to compress the frames into discrete tokens that represent patches of the video. The dynamics model then takes the tokens for the frames we’ve already seen, together with an action, and predicts the tokens for the next frame. We can decode those predicted tokens back into pixels.

In Genie, those actions are learned from video as well—they’re latent actions, rather than action labels supplied with the training data. So at generation time, choosing a latent action conditions how the next frame changes, which gives you a way to control the environment.

r001.rationale: It describes predicting discrete video tokens and decoding them to pixels, but does not state that this representation enables cross-entropy loss.

r002.rationale: It says the model predicts next-frame tokens, but does not mention masked token prediction as the training method.

sol-6.1.text: We first tokenize the video, so each frame becomes a grid of discrete tokens representing patches of that frame. The dynamics model then predicts the tokens for the next frame, conditioned on the previous frames and a latent action. So you can think of it as predicting video tokens instead of words, with the action telling the model how the scene should change. We then decode those predicted tokens back into pixels to produce the next frame.

r001.rationale: It says the model predicts discrete video tokens, but does not explain that this representation enables cross-entropy loss for patch prediction.

r002.rationale: It describes predicting next-frame tokens conditioned on previous frames and an action, but does not state that training uses masked token prediction.
